text: More than 5,000 years ago, people in Mesopotamia invented writing, and with it comes the first clear sign of their religion.
They wrote prayers and stories of their gods on clay tablets, in a script called cuneiform.
src: The first evidence of a recognisably Mesopotamian religion comes with the invention of writing around 3500 BCE
Its myths, prayers, incantations and lists of gods were written in cuneiform on clay tablets

text: They believed in many gods, among them the goddess Inanna, the moon god Nanna and the sun god Utu.
They believed that people had been made to serve the gods.
src: Among the greatest were Enlil, king of the gods, An (Akkadian Anu), Enki (Ea), the moon god Nanna (Sîn), the sun god Utu (Shamash) and Inanna
Humanity was believed to have been created to serve the gods

text: Every city had its own god, like Marduk at Babylon and Ashur at the city of Assur.
Each god was thought to live in its temple, where its statue was served meals twice a day.
src: Every city had its patron god, among them Enki at Eridu, Enlil at Nippur, Marduk at Babylon and Ashur at Assur
Each god lived in a temple in its city, often a stepped ziggurat, present in a cult image to which banquets were served twice a day

text: Priests tried to learn the wishes of the gods from birds, dreams and the sky.
Ordinary people prayed to a personal god, who they believed would protect them.
src: Priests read the will of the gods in entrails, birds, the sky and dreams
ordinary people prayed to a personal god / who from the 2nd millennium BCE was thought to protect them

text: King Hammurabi of Babylon raised the god Marduk to be one of the greatest gods.
More than 1,500 years ago the old religion faded, as most of its people became Christians.
src: King Hammurabi raised Marduk, until then of little importance, to supremacy alongside Anu and Enlil
it had almost completely died out by about 400–500 CE, after its indigenous adherents had largely become Syriac Christians

text: Its Epic of Gilgamesh tells of a king, his wild friend Enkidu and his search to live forever.
Many stories in the Bible, such as the Flood, may have been based on these older myths.
src: the story of the heroic king Gilgamesh, his wild friend Enkidu and his search for immortality
Many biblical stories found in Judaism, Christianity, Islam and Mandaeism were possibly based on earlier Mesopotamian myths: the creation, the Garden of Eden, the Flood
